title: Elastic reservoir capacity runbook for bursty inference workloads
author: Priya Raman
content:
Overview:

This runbook documents the Elastic Reservoir pattern we operate across the inference fleet to absorb short, high-amplitude traffic bursts without violating customer-facing SLOs. The pattern is designed for inference workloads (text generation, chat, embeddings) that have unpredictable burstiness due to external events (campaigns, viral features) and internal retry storms. The document explains detection signals, hedging policies (error budget-aware), automated mitigation actions, and manual escalation steps for SREs on-call.

Goals and scope:
- Maintain primary latency SLOs (P50/P90/P99) and availability SLOs for multi-tenant hosted API and Dedicated pools during short bursts (2–30 minutes).
- Prevent full-tenant evictions where possible; prefer graceful degradation (rate-limited tail, prompt-preserving routing).
- Limit cost by using short-duration reservoir capacity and prioritized tenant admission.
- Apply uniformly to: hosted inference API (front-end gateway + model-serving clusters), dedicated pools, and cross-region failover targets.

Key definitions:
- Reservoir capacity: transient pool of spare GPU instances or pre-warmed model workers assigned to absorb burst demand for up to B minutes.
- Hedging window: sliding time window used for short-term capacity estimation (default: 5 minutes).
- Emergency throttle: prioritized request shedder that enforces token-level and request-level limits to protect SLOs.
- SLO burn signal: percentage of error budget consumed in last X minutes (default X=60). High-burn triggers become part of decision rules.

Service-level targets (example baseline):
| Metric | Target | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| API availability (success rate) | 99.95% / 30d | Applies to hosted API token-scoped traffic |
| Latency P95 (generation) | < 350ms | Measured at edge for short responses (<=128 tokens) |
| Latency P99 (generation) | < 1200ms | Tail target guiding throttles and fallback |

Telemetry & detection signals:
- Primary signals (real-time):
  - Request rate per tenant / cluster (qps, tokens/s) sampled at 10s granularity.
  - Serving queue length and worker CPU/GPU utilization per model-variant.
  - Token processing latency histogram (P50/P90/P99) per route.
  - SLO burn rate: short-window error-budget consumption (5m, 1h).
  - Admission gateway rejections and 429 spikes.
- Secondary signals (supporting):
  - Upstream API key metadata (campaign tag, known marketing campaigns) from customer headers.
  - Recent config changes / rollouts in the last 60 minutes.

Automatic decision policy (priority order):
1) Detection: trigger when all of the following hold for hedging window (default 5m):
   - cluster-wide incoming token rate > baseline + 3 sigma (60m baseline), AND
   - model-serving queue depth > configured threshold for > 2 sampling intervals, AND
   - SLO burn rate for impacted tenant or cluster < 50% (we favor mitigation without exhausting budgets).
2) Pre-check: verify reservoir free capacity > 1 worker equivalent. If yes, allocate; otherwise proceed to controlled throttle.
3) Allocation: spin up reservoir workers (see "Runbook actions"), route a fraction of new requests to reservoir with probabilistic admission to avoid cache stampede.
4) Observability: create an ephemeral incident timeline entry and tag traces for the affected tenants/models. Notify on-call via existing pager channel and create an ephemeral Slack channel with auto-archive in 8 hours.

Runbook actions (automated + manual):
- Automated actions (system-initiated):
  1. Reservoir allocation: call internal actuator to attach N worker pods (N = min(ceil(delta_qps / worker_capacity), configured_max_burst)). Example CLI: redwoodctl reservoir allocate --cluster model-eu-1 --workers 6 --reason "burst-hedge"
  2. Localized routing: enable reservoir routing policy for target model-variants (route header X-Reservoir: true).
  3. Soft-throttle low-priority tokens: apply token-priority map, demote best-effort traffic to 10% of baseline.
  4. Activate degraded fast-path: switch generation mode to lower-memory quantized kernel on non-critical variants when latency tail is rising.
- Manual SRE checklist (if auto actions fail or SLOs continue to degrade):
  1. Confirm telemetry (dashboards: Reservoir Overview, Token QPS per tenant, P99 heatmap).
  2. Run reservoir status: redwoodctl reservoir status --cluster <cluster> (verify worker readiness).
  3. If allocation failed due to quota, escalate to capacity-oncall (pager ID: capacity-team) and request temporary quota increase for 30–120 minutes.
  4. If tenant-specific burst: coordinate with customer success to enable tenant-side rate limits or move tenant to dedicated queue.
  5. If cross-region fallback is required: follow cross-region failover playbook (step-by-step below).

Cross-region fallback (summary):
1) Validate that warm standby region has compatible model variant and quantization profile.
2) If standby capacity >= required workers, update routing policy to mirror 20% of traffic and monitor for 5 minutes.
3) Gradually increase mirrored traffic in 20% increments while observing P99.
4) If mirror test passes for 15 minutes, perform full shift with TTL-based DNS fallback and global edge reconfiguration.

Throttle & eviction policy (prioritization):
- Priority levels (high -> low): system-critical (control-plane), premium customers, standard tenants, best-effort tenants.
- Eviction order: best-effort -> standard non-paying -> standard paying under negotiated SLAs -> premium (last). Evictions should be explicit (owner notified) and tracked in the eviction ledger for 90 days.
- Throttle knobs: request-rate cap, token-rate cap, request concurrency cap. Provide examples: redwoodctl throttle set --tenant <id> --token-rate 500 --concurrency 8 --duration 15m

SLO-aware hedging guardrails:
- Never consume reservoir capacity for more than 20% of a tenant's monthly error budget without manual approval.
- If cluster SLO burn exceeds 70% in 1h window, halt automatic reservoir expansion and switch to conservative throttles + incident postmortem.
- Maintain a rolling list of emergency quotas for busy periods; each emergency quota must be approved by capacity-team lead and recorded.

Post-incident actions and evidence collection:
1) If the hedging event lasted > 10 minutes or caused > 1% SLO degradation, open a post-incident review (PIR) using the standard template.
2) Required artifacts for PIR: 10s QPS series, worker allocation timeline, traces for 100 sample slow tokens, reservoir allocator logs, admission gateway decisions, related customer contact history.
3) Tag PIR with mitigation decisions and any manual overrides (quota increases, manual evictions).

Operational tooling & dashboards referenced:
- Reservoir Overview (grafana): cluster, allocated_reservoir_workers, reservoir_fill_ratio, average_recovery_time
- Hedging Health (grafana): short-window burn, priority throttle rate, cross-region mirror success rate
- Traces: trace-service (filter tag: event:reservoir-hedge)
- CLI tooling: redwoodctl (reservoir allocate/status/release), admissionctl (throttle, priority-map), quotactl (request temporary quota)

Maintenance and runbook ownership:
- Runbook owner: Priya Raman (serving-runtime team).
- Capacity policy owner: Capacity Oncall / eng-sre.
- Review cadence: quarterly review and after any reservoir-triggered PIR.
- Test plan: monthly chaos drill (inject synthetic burst at 1.5x typical high percentile for 10m) to verify end-to-end allocation and routing.

Metrics to track for continuous improvement:
- Mean time to reservoir attach (goal < 60s).
- Fraction of bursts absorbed without tenant eviction (> 90%).
- Average SLO burn delta during hedging events (goal < 5% additional burn).
- False-positive hedges (events where reservoir allocated but not materially used) target < 15%.

Runbook appendix (example commands and JSON snippets):
- Allocate reservoir (example):
  redwoodctl reservoir allocate --cluster model-us-west-2 --workers 4 --reason "auto-hedge"
- Check status:
  redwoodctl reservoir status --cluster model-us-west-2 --json
- Example admission throttle JSON (used by admissionctl):
  {
    "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
    "token_rate": 1000,
    "concurrency": 12,
    "expires_at": "2026-11-03T12:45:00Z"
  }
